UN REPORT SAYS U.S. DRUG BOAT STRIKES MAY CONSTITUTE WAR CRIMES  WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR DEPLOYED TROOPS?

A United Nations human rights inquiry concluded that the U.S. military’s lethal kinetic strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in international waters may constitute war crimes and extrajudicial executions, as analyzed by Task & Purpose and The Guardian.

With over 68 targeted missile and gunship strikes killing at least 240 individuals aboard "go-fast" boats and semi-submersibles since the high-seas campaign began, the report has raised urgent questions for military personnel regarding what an international war crimes allegation means for the pilots, drone operators, and gunners ordered to pull the trigger.

The Legal Reality for U.S. Service Members
For frontline troops executing counter-narcotics operations under U.S. Southern Command, the UN findings create a high-stakes legal and moral dilemma:

The UCMJ "Manifestly Unlawful" Standard: Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice (Articles 90 and 92), service members have a binding legal duty to obey lawful orders. Troops are only legally permitted—and required—to disobey an order if it is "manifestly unlawful," meaning an act that a person of ordinary sense would immediately recognize as illegal on its face (such as shooting unarmed prisoners or deliberately targeting civilians).

The Intelligence Asymmetry Catch-22: Door gunners, Reaper drone pilots, and surface warfare tacticians do not produce legal determinations; they rely on classified intelligence and Staff Judge Advocate (JAG) target approvals declaring the vessels hostile narco-terrorist threats. A junior operator refusing a command based on an external UN report risks immediate relief for cause, non-judicial punishment, or court-martial for insubordination.

Domestic vs. International Legal Exposure: Domestically, service members who execute strikes in good faith under verified rules of engagement are protected from UCMJ prosecution under the defense of superior orders. Internationally, while the U.S. does not recognize International Criminal Court (ICC) jurisdiction over American troops, international war crimes designations generate diplomatic friction and heighten legal scrutiny for senior planners authorizing maritime strike doctrine.

Where do you stand on using military airstrikes against drug cartels on the high seas? Drop your vote below:

Cpl. Baughman was deployed with the 187th Infantry Regiment in September 2005 for a year-long deployment to Iraq. On July 17, 2006, Baughman's Humvee was part of a convoy participating in patrol operations in the city of Bayji, Iraq. His Humvee was hit by an RPG, severely injuring him. Later that day, Baughman died from his injuries.

On July 19, 2006, Baughman was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal and the Purple Heart for going beyond the call of duty and giving his life for his fellow soldiers.

Asked if Putin is a friend to America, Trump said this:
“I can’t speak to America.” 

At a White House news conference on November 20, President Trump was pressed on his relationship with Vladimir Putin.

He has repeatedly called Putin his “friend.”
When a reporter asked whether Putin is also a friend to the United States, Trump answered:
“I can’t speak to America.”

He went on to defend the personal relationship, saying he has a “fantastic” one with the Russian leader and that such relationships keep the country safer.

The exchange quickly stood out.
One moment Trump is describing a personal friendship.
The next he’s declining to say whether that friendship extends to the country he leads.

Supporters hear a president prioritizing personal diplomacy and results.
Critics hear a line that draws a strange separation between the president and the nation.

Either way, the quote is now out there.

What do you make of that answer?

SgtMaj Ramona D. Cook, #USMC, Retired, is honored by having her uniform displayed at Camp Pendleton's Historic Ranch House in recognition of Women's History Month. #SemperFidelis, SgtMaj.

#marinelife #Marine
Lcpl Joshua Alonzo, Lcpl Davenport, and Pvt. Heath Warner. They were KIA in Haqliniyah Iraq on November 22, 2006. Sleep well, Marines!

The U.S. government just released decades of archived "Bigfoot Files" — and the 1982 Forest Service report is raising eyebrows.

Buried in newly unsealed USDA records is a June 1982 investigation by Wildlife Biologist Rodney L. Johnson into 15-inch tracks found in Washington's Mill Creek Watershed inside the Umatilla National Forest.

After inspecting two sites, Johnson listed eight reasons he believed the prints were "made by something other than a 300 pound plus two footed being" — noting an unchanging four-foot stride regardless of slope, shallower imprints than his own boots, brushed-aside pine needles, and zero heel or toe slippage on steep mud.

Yet on the very next page, he admitted something remarkable — "If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail. The 'print' marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate. They appear very natural."

Elaborate 1982 hoax or something unexplained in the Pacific Northwest? Drop your take below.

#BigfootFiles #USForestService

“SEVEN BULLETS. A SHATTERED JAW. AND THE INDOMITABLE WILL TO WIN.” — In January 2008, Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office detective and SWAT operator Jared Reston chased a shoplifter outside a shopping mall. Seconds later, he took a point-blank .45 caliber round straight through his chin that shattered his lower jaw, followed by six more hits to his chest and limbs. Lying on his back in the dirt, Reston kept his vision focused, unholstered his Glock 22, and fought his way back to his feet to end the threat.

“That’s how law enforcement works: you can go from a foot chase to full-on fighting for your life in half a second. When you get shot in the face, you have two choices: lie there and die, or stay in the fight and win. My thought was simple: He’s not going home today, I am.”

— Detective Jared Reston, Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office & Medal of Valor Recipient

Tactical Breakdown: Surviving 7 Point-Blank Rounds
The Lethal Transition: Chasing an armed shoplifting suspect across a parking lot outside Regency Square Mall in Jacksonville, Florida, Reston closed the distance when the suspect spun with a stolen .45 ACP handgun, firing 12 rounds at point-blank range.

Absorbing Massive Trauma: Seven rounds struck Reston: one entered his chin and fractured his mandible into pieces, three rounds hit his concealed Kevlar vest directly over vital organs, and three more tore through his elbow, hip, and thigh.

Returning Fire from the Ground: Knocked violently onto his back in the mud and choking on blood, Reston refused to enter psychological shock. He cleared his holster, acquired his front sight, and fired 14 rounds from his Glock 22 (.40 S&W), hitting the advancing gunman repeatedly.

Closing the Distance & CNS Stop: Despite absorbing multiple torso hits, the suspect continued firing. Reston fought his way back onto his feet, closed to contact distance, and delivered immediate central nervous system headshots to terminate the threat.

Weapon-Mounted Light Standoff Advantage: During the grapple, the bezel of Reston's Streamlight weapon-mounted light extended past the muzzle, creating the mechanical standoff necessary to keep his pistol in battery and fire contact shots without jamming the slide.

The Road to the Medal of Valor: Following multiple reconstructive surgeries on his face and jaw, Reston returned to active SWAT service, was awarded the Florida Law Enforcement Officer of the Year, and received the Presidential Public Safety Officer Medal of Valor in Washington, D.C.

On Christmas Eve 2007, Royal Marines Commando Mark Ormrod was on a routine foot patrol in Helmand Province, Afghanistan, when he triggered a concealed improvised explosive device while moving to provide covering fire for his teammates.

Evacuated by helicopter to Camp Bastion and then flown to Birmingham, Ormrod lost both legs above the knee and his right arm above the elbow, becoming Britain's first triple amputee to survive the Afghanistan conflict. After waking up in the hospital, he proposed to his girlfriend, Becky, and she said yes.

Told he might never walk again, Ormrod spent years in rehabilitation learning to use prosthetics, left the Royal Marines in 2010, and went on to win multiple medals at the Invictus Games while advocating for wounded veterans.

#MarkOrmrod #RoyalMarines

A sobering crisis inside America's top intelligence and cyber commands is drawing urgent scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

At least 11 National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command workers — including military personnel and civilians, largely based at Fort Meade, Maryland — have died by suicide over roughly the past year.

Lawmakers are demanding answers and pushing for $11 million in mental health and resilience funding requested by NSA and Cyber Command leader Gen. Joshua Rudd, along with placing security-cleared counselors directly inside classified workspaces. While officials say each case involved complex personal factors, former insiders warn of relentless burnout from high-tempo "deployed-in-place" cyber operations.

Doris Miller, known as “Dorie” to shipmates and friends, was a U.S. Navy Sailor recognized for his bravery during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. He was the first African American recipient of the Navy Cross.

Developing out of the Persian Gulf — air raid sirens are sounding and loud explosions are being heard in Bahrain amid initial reports that Iran has launched drones toward U.S. bases.

Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, has already intercepted three waves of Iranian drone attacks in recent days targeting U.S. radar and military installations at Al-Riffa and Sheikh Isa air bases, prompting U.S. retaliatory precision strikes on an IRGC missile site on Qeshm Island earlier this week.

We are monitoring CENTCOM and Bahraini officials for confirmation on interceptions, damage, or casualties as the situation develops.

Follow for live updates as more details come in.

#Bahrain #Iran #USMilitary

NIGHT COLLISION OFF CORONADO. INJURED IN THE CRASH, HE DIVED INTO TOTAL DARKNESS TO PULL HIS BROTHER OUT.

Operating at speed in the open ocean at midnight leaves zero room for error.

Returning from nighttime tactical training off Southern California with Naval Special Warfare Logistics Support Unit 1, a special operations support boat struck a submerged rock jetty in the dark. The violent impact ejected crew members into the freezing surf, leaving one sailor knocked unconscious and floating facedown in pitch-black waters.

Injured and concussed from the initial collision himself, Utilitiesman 1st Class Steven Schumacher saw his teammate in the black chop. Disregarding his own trauma, Schumacher dove straight over the gunwale into the Pacific, fought the swell to reach his unresponsive teammate, and hauled his brother back aboard to clear his airway until emergency medical teams arrived.

According to the official ceremony announcement from Navy.mil, Schumacher received the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for heroism under life-threatening conditions.

Diving into freezing black ocean water while bleeding and injured to save a teammate defines brotherhood in the special warfare community.

Col. Lewis Millett
Lewis Millett joined the Army in 1941 but got tired of waiting for the U.S. to invade someone, so he deserted to Canada and got himself deployed to London. When American entered the war, he jumped back under the Stars and Bars and twice saved men in his unit from certain death before his desertion charges caught up with him.

Lewis Millett joined the Army in 1941 but got tired of waiting for the U.S. to invade someone, so he deserted to Canada and got himself deployed to London. When America entered the war, he jumped back under the Stars and Bars and twice saved men in his unit from certain death before his desertion charges caught up with him.

He led an assault under fire in Panama in 1989.
37 years later, he finally got the medal. 
In December 1989, during Operation Just Cause, then-First Lieutenant Robert Gaddis was in the middle of the fight in Panama.

He led ambushes against enemy vehicles under heavy fire.
He moved alone through defensive positions.
He took command of a stalled assault and personally led the attack that cleared the objective.

Two days later, when Panamanian forces counterattacked with automatic weapons, mortars, and grenades, he helped move wounded soldiers and civilians to safety while continuing to direct his troops.

On November 19, 2026 — nearly 37 years later — retired Col. Robert Gaddis finally received the Bronze Star Medal with “V” device for valor.

Some awards arrive quickly.
This one took a lifetime.

Better late than never… but why did it take so long?

President Trump says he plans to make a "permanent" deal with Iran — one that no future U.S. president can undo.

Speaking with Fox News on Saturday, Trump said any agreement must permanently block Tehran from ever acquiring a nuclear weapon, downplaying regime change while noting the U.S. is now dealing with a third group of Iranian leadership.

Meanwhile, Qatari mediators met with officials in Tehran today as Iran demands an end to the U.S. naval blockade and refuses to ship its 60%-enriched uranium abroad — and Israeli officials warn Iran is rapidly rebuilding its missile production underground.

Should the U.S. lock in a permanent diplomatic deal with Iran, or is the risk of broken terms too high? Drop your take below.

#Trump #Iran #ForeignPolicy

In 2004, US Marine 1stSgt. Brad Kasal was engaged in a firefight with insurgents during the Second Battle of Fallujah. He was hit by seven 7.62mm rounds and 47 pieces of shrapnel from a fragmentation grenade. While fighting, he used his body to shield another Marine. He was responsible for saving the lives of several Marines under his command. After being taken out of the house by his Marines, he was still holding his M9 Beretta pistol and his Ka-Bar knife. He refused to lie on a litter to deny the enemy the satisfaction of seeing him in a supine position. After arriving at the field hospital, it was determined that he had lost 60% of his blood. It was later determined that he had over 100 puncture wounds. As a result of his injuries, he lost four inches of bone in his right leg. He has undergone 21 surgeries to repair the injuries to his leg. For his actions, he was awarded several medals, including the Navy Cross for valor. He retired in 2018 from the Marine Corps at the rank of Sgt. Major.

Russian missiles just crashed inside a NATO country.

On November 20, during a major Russian attack on Ukraine, two missiles and a jet-powered drone crossed into eastern Poland and came down on Polish soil.

No one was hurt.
But the objects landed inside NATO territory.

Polish leaders are calling it an intentional provocation, noting the timing and proximity to ongoing military exercises by Ukraine’s allies.
NATO scrambled jets and condemned the airspace violations.

This is not the first time debris or drones from the war have crossed the border.
It is, however, another clear reminder of how close the fighting sits to the alliance’s eastern flank.

The question now is what comes next.
Stronger statements? More air defense? A clearer red line?

Russian missiles falling on NATO soil — even without casualties — forces a response.

What should NATO do now?

“THE BRAVEST THING I HAVE EVER SEEN IN 17 YEARS HAPPENED ON THAT NIGHT.” — DEVGRU / SEAL Team 6 Operator DJ Shipley on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the rawest combat breakdowns in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show, former DEVGRU assault team operator DJ Shipley recounted the night in Iraq when heavy machine-gun fire caught his team in open ground, leaving teammates gravely wounded in the dark.

In his own words:

“I remember looking over and seeing Jay [Jason Redman]. I remember him sitting upright, and I watched him get shot one more time, right in the face. He hit the ground so hard you knew he was dead.

We’re stuck behind a tractor tire that’s halfway out of the ground, serving no purpose, taking fire from every angle. It’s pitch black.

The bravest thing I have ever seen in 17 years happened on that night.

I watched Maddie get up and run forward after he had already been shot. He grabs our corpsman and starts dragging him backwards. Just like in the movies, the corpsman pulls his pistol, shooting into the woodline.

Maddie gets shot again—it spins him around and dumps him. He gets back up, grabs him, and gets shot again. Dumps him, gets back up, and continues dragging him until we got them all behind that tire.

Jason took one to the face that basically removed his jaw, removed his nose, and you could look inside him. Maddie’s arm was completely shattered. We basically just dog-piled on top of them. Plates on plates, just trying to build up a human wall so our brothers wouldn't take another bullet.”

Against all medical odds, Jason Redman survived the devastating facial gunshot wound, enduring dozens of reconstructive surgeries and going on to inspire millions across the veteran community.

Getting shot, knocked to the dirt, getting back up under machine-gun fire, and continuing to drag your wounded brothers to cover is the purest embodiment of brotherhood under fire.

Marriner Richards was a 19-year-old United States Marine from Syracuse, Utah, remembered by his family as a natural leader who was always willing to lend an ear to those in need. Stationed at the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms, California, his promising young life took a sudden turn on the night of Friday, November 6, 2026. After visiting the nearby Tortoise Rock Casino on the edge of the Mojave Desert, he walked away on foot without a vehicle, vanishing into the night. When he failed to return to his post, military police reported him missing the following day, launching a desperate two-week search across the vast and unforgiving desert terrain bordering Joshua Tree National Park.

Determined to bring their son home, Marriner's parents, Brock and Brooke Richards, traveled from Utah to California to join the search on the ground. They were met with an outpouring of love and support as dozens of local residents, fellow Marines, law enforcement deputies with off-road vehicles and helicopters, and even neighbors and church members who drove down from Utah banded together to comb the desert. For two agonizing weeks, volunteers searched tirelessly in the hopes of finding him safe. That hope came to a heartbreaking end on Friday, November 20, when a member of the search party discovered Marriner's body inside an abandoned building just a few miles from both the casino and his base. The San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department later confirmed the tragic news that the young Marine had died by suicide, leaving his family, his community in Utah, and his fellow service members mourning a life lost far too soon.

Maj. Gen. Lawrence L. Wells, 9th Air Force commander, presents the Silver Star to Tiffany Smith, widow of Senior Airman Bradley Smith (far right) during a ceremony Sept. 8, 2012, in Troy, Ill. Smith spent only a few weeks with his new daughter, Chloe, now almost age 3, before deploying to Afghanistan where just months later he was killed by an IED during a firefight. As a Tactical Air Control Party member, or TACP, Brad was part of a two-man team assigned to support a 13-man Army platoon and was trained to call in close air support should the men come under fire and need the battlefield neutralized from above.

Two completely different takes on the same diplomatic table.

After U.S. President Donald Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China as his "friend," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pushed back in a CNN interview — "For us, he is an enemy, and of course, for us, he is a killer."

At the White House on Friday, Trump defended his approach, saying he has a "fantastic relationship" with Putin that gives Washington "a lot of additional strength" as it pushes for a diplomatic end to the war. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy noted that despite the divide over rhetoric, the United States remains "the strongest mediator" Ukraine can have.

Should U.S. leaders maintain warm personal rapport with adversaries to negotiate peace, or draw a harder public line? Drop your thoughts below.

#UkraineRussiaWar #Zelenskyy #Trump

Hacked again — and this time, attackers targeted the FBI's nationwide crime database.

According to CNN, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), the core system used by police departments and federal agencies across the country to check warrants, criminal histories, and background records.

It's the second reported intrusion in just a few months, following September's ShinyHunters breach of an FBI jobs website — and it comes right as federal officials have been trying to reassure the public after a wave of high-profile outages across banks, the NSA, and air traffic control systems.

If even the FBI's own databases are getting hit twice in one fall, how confident are you in federal cybersecurity right now? Drop your thoughts below.

#FBI #Cybersecurity #NCIC

“3,540 METERS. THE BULLET WAS IN THE AIR FOR ALMOST TEN SECONDS BEFORE IMPACT.” — JTF2 Sniper Dallas Alexander on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most iconic long-range ballistics breakdowns in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episodes #047 & #050), former Canadian Tier 1 Joint Task Force 2 (JTF2) sniper Dallas Alexander detailed the world-record combat kill in Mosul, Iraq—engaging an ISIS machine-gun crew from over 2.2 miles away.

In his own words:

“When you look through the glass at 3,540 meters, you aren’t just looking down a street—you’re looking across entire cities. You’re factoring in the curvature of the earth, the temperature of the air, the mirage, crosswinds between multiple mountain corridors, and Coriolis effect.

We spotted the target on a rooftop engaging coalition forces. The range was so extreme that nobody had ever even attempted an engagement at that distance in combat history.

My spotter did the calculations. We dialed the elevation so high that the barrel was literally pointing into the sky above the skyline.

Squeeze the trigger. Boom.

The bullet left the chamber, and then you wait. At that distance, the round doesn’t hit instantly. It flew for nearly ten full seconds. You have enough time to breathe, blink, reset your sight picture, and have a brief conversation with your spotter while the bullet is traveling across the sky.

Ten seconds later: Impact. Target drops instantly.

When the confirmation came through, we didn’t celebrate. You just look at each other in absolute disbelief that physics allowed that to happen.”

Firing a .50 BMG McMillan TAC-50 from a high-rise rooftop during the 2017 siege of Mosul, Alexander and his spotter smashed the previous world record by more than 1,000 meters—saving dozens of allied troops pinned down below.

Waiting ten full seconds for a bullet to cross the sky and strike an enemy position over two miles away pushes the boundaries of human precision and physics.

Flying for Thanksgiving next week? U.S. security officials just put airlines on high alert.

On Friday, the FBI, DHS, and TSA sent a joint advisory to U.S. airlines, cargo carriers, and airports warning of Al-Qaeda-linked calls for hijacking attacks modeled on a Flydubai attempt. The timing is no coincidence — AAA estimates around 6 million Americans will fly domestically between November 24 and November 30.

Officials emphasized there is no known specific, credible threat underway right now, and bulletins like this are routinely shared with carriers ahead of peak travel. Still, crews and airport staff are being told to watch closely for anyone probing security procedures or missing airline badges, radios, and uniforms.

Are you flying next week, and does an alert like this make you feel safer knowing agencies are watching — or more nervous at the airport? Let us know below.

#TSA #DHS #FBI #AviationSecurity

Nine people lost their lives on that plane — and the person on the other end of the radio carries it too.

An unconfirmed report says the air traffic controller who was working the Learjet 60 that crashed in Palm Beach County on November 1 is seeking permanent disability, saying the trauma has left him unable to return to the scope. While that claim hasn't been officially confirmed, anyone who has ever sat in that chair knows how heavy those final mayday calls are.

My grandfather spent 25 years in New York air traffic control and put it plainly — "you never forget it." Every controller knows that when an emergency unfolds in real time over the headset, you stay calm, do everything by the book, and still live with the silence after the radar target disappears.

Do we talk enough about mental health and trauma support for air traffic controllers? Share your thoughts — or a story if you've worked in aviation — in the comments.

#AirTrafficControl #Aviation

Less than two weeks away — Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan is scheduled to face a U.S. Army firing squad on December 3, 2026.

Seventeen years after the November 5, 2009 attack that killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas, the military's first execution since 1961 — and first firing squad since 1945 — is set for 1 p.m. CST. President Donald Trump approved the death sentence in early October following a recommendation from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the U.S. Supreme Court previously declined to hear Hasan's appeal in 2025.

Ahead of the date, Killeen ISD announced all schools and district facilities will close on December 3 as a precaution.

After more than a decade of appeals, does this scheduled execution bring long-overdue justice for the Fort Hood families? Share your thoughts below.

#FortHood #NidalHasan #USArmy

Up to $150 MILLION a year at risk—and an internal government memo basically admits they can’t stop it. 🚨💰

A bombshell ProPublica investigation just uncovered a 25-page internal Labor Department memo detailing the agency’s inability to police fraud in the federal program meant to care for civilian contractors wounded in war zones.

Under the system, private insurers pay out war-hazard injury claims and then bill the U.S. government for reimbursement. Between 2018 and 2024, insurer reimbursement applications jumped eightfold—from around 1,000 to more than 8,000—with billions flowing to major carriers since 2014.

Meanwhile, the memo warns that questionable medical evidence is often overlooked, insurers sometimes settle dubious claims fast knowing taxpayers will reimburse them, and one former top official estimates up to $150 million every year is at risk.

The Labor Department says its hands are tied by decades-old laws and that real reform requires Congress to act.

Why do government reimbursement programs keep getting left wide open to abuse before anyone fixes the rules? Drop your take below. 👇

U.S. intel: Iran may be planning a dirty bomb in Washington.
Trump’s response: “We wipe them out.” 

According to seven U.S. officials who spoke to CNN, American intelligence has picked up Iranian planning related to a potential dirty bomb or chemical attack targeting senior officials in Washington, D.C.

Officials stress this appears to be about developing options rather than an imminent attack.
The White House says there is currently no credible threat to the homeland.

Still, the reporting is specific enough that it triggered contingency planning on the U.S. side.

President Trump’s reaction was blunt.
He said if Iran moves forward with something like this, they will “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before.”

Tensions with Iran have already been extremely high.
This latest intelligence adds another layer of risk to an already volatile situation.

Is this serious contingency planning by Tehran… or something closer to an active threat?

A #Marine infantry battalion that was embroiled in a war-zone scandal will present a former squad leader with the nation's third-highest valor award this week — nearly five years after he led his comrades out of an intense firefight in Afghanistan.

Former Sgt. Matthew Parker, who served as a squad leader with 3rd Battalion, 2nd Marines, during the unit's 2011 deployment to Afghanistan, will be presented with the Silver Star on Friday during a ceremony at #CampLejeune, North Carolina, Marine Corps Times has learned.

Parker is being recognized for stepping up to lead his platoon when his commander and another squad leader were injured in an attack while operating in Helmand province's Musa Qala district, according to his award citation.

While Parker's actions serve as an example of the success 3/2 showed on the battlefield during what was highly held as a successful deployment, much of it was overshadowed when a video surfaced in 2012 showing other Marines with his unit defiling enemy remains.

Parker was not involved, but his award nomination — along with several other personnel matters within the unit — was put on administrative hold, said 1st Lt. Joe Caldwell, a Marine spokesman.

The award then had to go through the approval process, Caldwell added. Parker's Silver Star was approved by Commandant Gen. Robert Neller on Dec. 31.

On May 21, 2011, Parker and his platoon were attacked by an entrenched enemy force. The insurgents were armed with small arms, machine guns, anti-tank-style weapons and grenade launchers.

When the Marines' platoon commander and another squad leader were injured in the attack, Parker sprang into action.
"Sergeant Parker boldly assumed control as the ground force commander of two rifle squads, a combined anti-armor team section, a vehicle mobile element and a sniper team," the award citation states.

Under a barrage of enemy fire, Parker coordinated the platoon's maneuvers until they were able to strike the enemy from three directions. When the insurgents hit back with intense machine gun and recoilless rifle fire, Parker "calmly and precisely coordinated for close-air support and high-mobility artillery rocket system strikes that destroyed two enemy machine gun positions," his citation states.

He seized that opportunity to guide supporting fires while continuing to direct his Marines. As a result, the enemy was forced to withdraw.

Parker helped evacuate the wounded Marines, despite continued sporadic fire from the insurgents as they withdrew. He led the Marines to safety at the closest patrol base.
"By his zealous initiative, courageous actions and exceptional dedication to duty, Sergeant Parker reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service," his citation states.

Parker was not the only member of 3/2 to be nominated for a valor award during that deployment. One of the snipers involved in the controversial video was put up for a Bronze Star with combat device, but that award has never been issued.
That Marine's sniper platoon was credited with killing hundreds of insurgents and integrating tanks into their missions — a highly successful move outside of normal sniper doctrine. The Corps' top leaders visited the team downrange that fall to congratulate the Marines on their accomplishments.

Parker could not immediately be reached for comment about his award. He medically retired from the #MarineCorps in February 2015, according to a Marine official.

KHILLIGAY, Afghanistan – U.S. Army Sgt. Joshua R. Labbe of the 10th Mountain Division's 1st Brigade Combat Team received the Silver Star medal, the nation's third highest award for valor in combat, on Feb. 16, during a ceremony at Forward Operating Base Khilligay in northern Afghanistan.

Labbe, from Stonington, Conn., an infantry squad leader with 1st Battalion, 87th Infantry Regiment, is credited with saving the life of one soldier and protecting numerous soldiers during a complex attack that lasted more than six hours.

“We are here to recognize the sacrifice and courage of the soldiers and leaders in Shafi Khel on Oct. 6,” said Lt. Col. Russell Lewis, 1-87 commander, said during the ceremony. “Sgt. Labbe is a hero. He didn't go out on Oct. 6 to earn an award — he just did his job. Except his job that day called for extraordinary actions and he stepped up and helped his comrades.”

On Oct. 6, 2010, Labbe's platoon was conducting a joint combat patrol in the village of Shafi Khel, Baghlan province, Afghanistan, with their Afghan national security force partners.

While establishing an observation post on a hilltop, Labbe and soldiers from 1st Squad as well as the mortar team, came under enemy fire. Initially, the enemy attacked the soldiers of 3rd Platoon with rocket-propelled grenades.
“One truck of ours was hit by an RPG,” Labbe said. “When I saw that truck get hit, I immediate started suppressing with the mortar system.”

Over the next four hours, the platoon came under RPG and small arms fire. Labbe directed the soldiers on the hill to return fire with multiple weapons systems. The hilltop then came under sniper fire, forcing Labbe and the other soldiers to take cover in holes they had dug.

Later, Labbe was told to collapse their position on the hilltop and return to the base of the hill where the remainder of his platoon was located.

“I had to get out of my hole and run to the other hole where the mortar system was,” he said. “When I got to the hole, I got everyone one up, got them online, and got everybody ready. As soon as we got out of the hole, we got sniper fire again.”

With three of the five soldiers making it across the hill to the other hole safely, Labbe and Pfc. Parker Radatz had returned to the mortar hole due to the accuracy of the sniper fire. Labbe and Radatz gathered themselves and attempted to get across the hill again.

“I ran to my hole thinking he was right beside me; little did I know he had actually tripped and fell,” Labbe said. “I turned around, and I saw him trying to get his composure to get back up, but he couldn't because there were multiple rounds impacting all around him.”

With complete disregard for his own safety, Labbe ran across the exposed hilltop to the fallen soldier through enemy fire, picked him up, and brought him to safety.

“I just did what I had to in that situation,” Labbe said. “He has people that care for him and love him, I knew I had to go pick him up and get him to safety. It's my job to take care of my men.”

Later, as the platoon moved down the road, the tow bar pulling the battle-damaged vehicle snapped. While Labbe and three soldiers began repairing the tow bar, once again, the platoon came under small arms fire from nearby rooftops and walls. Labbe immediately returned fire with his M4 rifle.

The small arms fire discontinued for a moment, allowing Labbe to run back to his vehicle to retrieve an M249 machine gun. He moved to a position allowing him to pull security down the alleyway and the walls where they had received fire. At this point, the enemy hopped over the walls and began engaging the platoon again.

With the enemy less than 20 meters away, Labbe stood completely exposed on the road and continued to shield the recovery crew as he fired the machine gun from his shoulder. After expending the 200-round ammunition pouch, he fired the weapon using his 30-round M4 rifle magazines.

“I engaged them for roughly two minutes and continued to pull security until the tow bar was fixed,” he said.

Once the vehicle was recovered, 3rd Platoon continued down the road, where they were ambushed. While still in close contact with the enemy, another vehicle suddenly plunged into an irrigation ditch. Labbe immediately dismounted and moved under fire to the stuck vehicle.

He coordinated the evacuation and recovery of the vehicle while still being engaged with RPG and machinegun fire from compounds and tree lines from less than 100 meters away. Labbe remained exposed to the enemy until the rest of the platoon recovered the vehicle and mounted back in their trucks.

“I feel honored to receive the Silver Star,” he said. “However, I don't think just my actions alone allowed us to be victorious that day. It was the whole platoon. Everyone who was out there that day played an important role in getting everyone back here alive. I couldn't have done what I did that day without my brothers in 3rd Platoon.”

Over the course of more than six hours of close combat, Labbe went above and beyond the call of duty as a squad leader.

“Today, we recognize his actions because they are not common,” said Lewis. “His actions that day distinguished him from others and truly impacted the outcome of the fight in Shafi Khel.”

The President of the United States of America, authorized by Title 10, Section 8742, U.S.C., awards the Air Force Cross to Senior Airman Jason D. Cunningham for extraordinary heroism in military operations against an opposing armed force while serving as a pararescueman near the village of Marzak in the Paktia Province of Afghanistan on 4 March 2002.

On that proud day, Airman Cunningham was the primary Air Force Combat Search and Rescue medic assigned to a Quick Reaction Force tasked to recover two American servicemen evading capture in austere terrain occupied by massed Al Qaida and Taliban forces.

Shortly before landing, his MH-47E helicopter received accurate rocket-propelled grenade and small arms fire, severely disabling the aircraft and causing it to crash land. The assault force formed a hasty defense and immediately suffered three fatalities and five critical casualties.

Despite effective enemy fire, and at great risk to his own life, Airman Cunningham remained in the burning fuselage of the aircraft in order to treat the wounded. As he moved his patients to a more secure location, mortar rounds began to impact within fifty feet of his position. Disregarding this extreme danger, he continued the movement and exposed himself to enemy fire on seven separate occasions.

When the second casualty collection point was also compromised, in a display of uncommon valor and gallantry, Airman Cunningham braved an intense small arms and rocket-propelled grenade attack while repositioning the critically wounded to a third collection point. Even after he was mortally wounded and quickly deteriorating, he continued to direct patient movement and transferred care to another medic.

In the end, his distinct efforts led to the successful delivery of ten gravely wounded Americans to life-saving medical treatment. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, and in the dedication of his service to his country, Senior Airman Cunningham reflected the highest credit upon himself and the United States #AirForce.

Small-arms fire rained down on the men of Company F, 2nd Battalion, 23rd Marines. Both Iraqi civilians and Marines were injured. Pinned down, with the injured needing assistance, Sgt. Scott C. Montoya rushed through enemy fire while "repeatedly exposing himself to fire-swept streets," according to his Navy Cross award citation.

Montoya received the U.S. military's second-highest award at Camp Pendleton for heroism stemming from his actions on April 8, 2003, two weeks into Operation Iraqi Freedom.

With his firearm in one hand engaging the enemy and a badly bleeding Marine in the other, he fought their way 500 yards to safety. He returned to the crossfire again and dragged another - who'd been dazed by the concussion of a grenade blast - to a casualty collection point. In all, he rescued four injured Marines and one Iraqi civilian out of harm's way, according to his citation.

Montoya's "extraordinary heroism" arose out of the battle for Baghdad.

Montoya described it this way:

"I saw a hurt Marine, and all my training came into play. It wasn't a cognitive thing; I just saw the situation and cared for my Marines."
Sgt. Jose N. Sanchez, a supply clerk with 2/23, has known Montoya for six years and wasn't surprised when he heard the news.

"The level he went - it's above and beyond the call of anyone, even a Marine," Sanchez said, adding: "What matters to him are his Marines, not the awards or the actions he took."

Montoya received the award in front of family, friends, and the men of his unit. Orange County Sheriff Michael S. Carona was also present.

When an enemy soldier stepped out behind a comrade, prepared to fire, M/Sgt. Mize killed him, saving the life of his fellow soldier. After rejoining the platoon, moving from man to man, distributing ammunition, and shouting words of encouragement he observed a friendly machine gun position overrun. He immediately fought his way to the position, killing 10 of the enemy and dispersing the remainder. Fighting back to the command post, and finding several friendly wounded there, he took a position to protect them. Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.
